stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS ROUT, WTI SINKS BELOW $78 ON IRAN DEAL HOPES
stories.body: WTI fell more than 4% to roughly $77.50, a fourth straight losing session and the lowest since early March, after a 4.9% slide Monday. Crude has now shed over 9% in two days.
stories.explain: Traders are unwinding the geopolitical 'war premium' priced in after recent Gulf tensions. Reports of a preliminary U.S.-Iran framework that would keep the Strait of Hormuz open removed the tail risk of a supply shock through a chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of seaborne oil, so the spot price reverts toward fundamentals-driven levels in the high-$70s.

stories.headline: FED OPENS WARSH-ERA MEETING, HOLD WIDELY EXPECTED WEDNESDAY
stories.body: The FOMC began its first meeting under new Chair Kevin Warsh, with markets pricing a hold in the 3.50%-3.75% target range. The decision and Warsh's debut press conference land Wednesday.
stories.explain: Warsh has historically leaned hawkish on inflation and skeptical of large balance sheets, so the focus is less on this hold than on the dot plot and tone for cuts later in 2026. With the 10Y near 4.47% and oil's drop easing near-term inflation fears, any dovish signal on the path could steepen the curve and lift rate-sensitive equities.

stories.headline: DOW HITS RECORD ABOVE 52,000 AS TECH ROTATES LOWER
stories.body: The Dow rose 0.64% to a record 52,003 on strength in financials and industrials, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.41% to 7,523 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.86% as chip and megacap tech names led the pullback.
stories.explain: This is a classic rotation: capital is leaving crowded, high-multiple tech and flowing into cyclical and value names that benefit from falling energy costs and a steady-rate backdrop. The divergence — a record Dow against a weak Nasdaq — signals breadth broadening rather than an index-wide selloff, a healthier internal posture than narrow megacap leadership.

stories.headline: U.S.-IRAN FRAMEWORK EASES STRAIT OF HORMUZ SUPPLY FEARS
stories.body: Hopes for a preliminary U.S.-Iran agreement that keeps the Strait of Hormuz open drove the cross-asset move: oil down sharply, gold holding above $4,300, and the dollar firmer with DXY near 99.35.
stories.explain: The Strait is the single most important oil chokepoint, so removing the threat of closure compresses risk premia across energy, safe-haven gold, and FX simultaneously. Gold's resilience despite the de-escalation reflects persistent central-bank buying and rate-cut expectations, while the firmer dollar reflects relief flows back into U.S. assets.

stories.headline: WELLS FARGO LIFTS YEAR-END S&P 500 TARGET
stories.body: Wells Fargo raised its year-end S&P 500 target, citing improving earnings momentum and easing macro risks, even as strategists flagged crowded tech positioning and sticky inflation as lingering concerns.
stories.explain: Sell-side target hikes mid-year typically follow upward revisions to forward EPS estimates rather than multiple expansion. With energy costs falling and the Fed expected to hold, margin assumptions improve, but the explicit warning on 'crowded tech bets' echoes today's rotation and the broader caution that warning indicators are flashing.

stories.headline: KENTUCKY LANDS TOP TRANSFER MOMCILOVIC AS PORTAL CLOSES
stories.body: Kentucky won the recruitment of Iowa State's Milan Momcilovic, the No. 1-rated transfer (48.7% on threes), over Louisville and Arizona. Over 2,700 players entered the now-closed portal; the NBA Draft runs June 23-24.

stories.headline: KNICKS WIN FIRST TITLE IN 53 YEARS, BRUNSON UNANIMOUS FINALS MVP
stories.body: New York beat San Antonio 4-1, rallying from double-digit deficits in all four wins. Jalen Brunson averaged 32.6 points and dropped 45 in the Game 5 clincher to take Finals MVP on all 11 votes.

stories.headline: BLOCKBUSTER OFFSEASON: GARRETT TO RAMS, A.J. BROWN TO PATRIOTS
stories.body: Two June 1 trades sent edge rusher Myles Garrett from Cleveland to the Rams and receiver A.J. Brown from Philadelphia to New England, giving QB Drake Maye a No. 1 target. Teams now break until late-July camp.

stories.headline: PORTAL CLOSES WITH LSU ON TOP; COACHES OPEN 2028 CONTACT
stories.body: Lane Kiffin's LSU holds the top-ranked transfer class after Auburn WR Cam Coleman, the No. 1 overall portal prospect, entered. June 15 marked the first day coaches could directly contact the class of 2028.

deepDive.title: Unwinding the War Premium: How Geopolitics Gets Priced Into Crude
content: Crude oil rarely moves on barrels alone. Over two sessions WTI shed more than 9%, falling below $78, not because supply suddenly surged or demand collapsed, but because a single tail risk was repriced. Reports of a preliminary U.S.-Iran framework that would keep the Strait of Hormuz open pulled the rug from under the 'war premium' — the extra dollars traders pay to insure against a supply shock that may never arrive. Watching the tape today is a lesson in how expectations, not just physical fundamentals, set the marginal price of a commodity.

The mechanism runs through expected value. A price reflects probability-weighted outcomes: if markets assign, say, a 20% chance to a Hormuz disruption that would spike oil $30, the spot price carries roughly $6 of embedded insurance. Collapse that probability toward zero and the premium evaporates almost instantly, even though not one extra barrel has shipped. That is why crude can crater 5% in a single session on a headline — the adjustment is to the distribution of outcomes, and option-implied volatility deflates alongside it as the fat left tail is trimmed.

The Strait of Hormuz is the reason this chokepoint matters more than most. Roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil threads through a passage only about 21 miles wide at its narrowest, with no easy substitute route for much of that flow. Economists call this convenience yield — the premium holders pay for physical oil precisely because it cannot be instantly replaced if a chokepoint closes. History rhymes here: the 1980s Tanker War and repeated Gulf flashpoints all show the same pattern of premium inflating on threat and bleeding out on de-escalation.

Tie it back to today's screen and the cross-asset coherence is the tell. Oil collapses, the dollar firms toward 99.35, and gold holds above $4,300 rather than tumbling — each asset repricing the same easing of geopolitical risk through its own channel. For the Fed opening its meeting under Kevin Warsh, cheaper energy quietly loosens the near-term inflation constraint, giving cover for a steadier rate path. One diplomatic headline thus ripples from a Gulf shipping lane to Treasury yields and a future mortgage rate.
